name: Solder two wires together
blurb: A good joint is shiny, concave and mechanically sound. The core insight is that you heat the work, not the solder — beginners nearly always get this backwards.
gear: Helping hands, side cutters, heat-shrink tubing
steps: Set the iron to around 350 °C and tin the tip: melt a little solder onto it and wipe on brass wool.
Prepare the wires: strip them, twist the strands, and tin each one separately.
Join them — a lineman’s splice or a hook joint, mechanically sound before soldering.
Heat the joint with the iron and feed solder into the joint, not onto the iron. The solder should flow in by capillary action.
Remove heat and hold still while it solidifies. A frosty, lumpy joint means it moved or was too cold.
Insulate with heat-shrink, slid on before you soldered, and tug-test the finished joint.
tips: A dull, grey blob is a cold joint and will fail. Reheat and add flux.
Never solder live circuits, work in ventilation, and wash your hands afterwards.
Keep the tip tinned. An oxidised black tip will not transfer heat and makes everything harder.
proof: Two joints that are shiny and smooth, survive a firm tug, and are neatly heat-shrunk.
